title: Use reference images to guide video generation (Veo on Vertex AI)
claims: Veo 3.1 takes one to three subject reference images (referenceType asset), JPEG or PNG; the images should show a single person, character or product.
With subject images veo-3.1-generate-001 returns 8 second videos only; aspect 16:9 or 9:16.
The page gives no advice on angles, lighting or image quality for references.

title: Magic Mirror: ID-Preserved Video Generation in Video Diffusion Transformers
claims: Uses a dual-branch face extractor (identity plus structure) and a light adapter with Conditioned Adaptive Normalization on a video DiT.
Two-stage training: synthetic identity pairs first, then video data; claims identity kept with dynamic motion and few extra parameters.

title: ID-Animator: Zero-Shot Identity-Preserving Human Video Generation
claims: A face adapter on a frozen video backbone makes a person video from a single reference face image, with no per-subject training.
Trained with a random-reference strategy and an ID-preserving loss; works with community AnimateDiff backbones.

title: Stand-In: A Lightweight and Plug-and-Play Identity Control for Video Generation
publisher: Bowen Xue et al. (WeChat Vision, Tencent; Nankai University)
claims: Adds a conditional image branch to a pretrained video model; identity is steered by restricted self-attention with conditional position mapping.
About 1% extra parameters and about 2,000 training pairs; claims better identity and quality than full-parameter training.
Extends to face swap, pose-referenced and stylised generation.
notes: Title and authors corrected after an independent search on 2026-11-08 (the first entry had the title from memory). The abstract describes the ~1% extra parameters; the training-pair count was not re-checked. Built on Wan2.1-14B text-to-video.

title: IP-Adapter: Text Compatible Image Prompt Adapter for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
claims: A 22M-parameter adapter with decoupled cross-attention (separate paths for text and image features) on a frozen diffusion model.
Because the base model is frozen it works with custom models of the same base and with other control tools; image and text prompts combine.

title: InstantID: Zero-shot Identity-Preserving Generation in Seconds
claims: Needs one face image and no per-subject training; an IdentityNet combines face embedding, landmark image and text.
Works with SD1.5 and SDXL community models in one forward pass; avoids the storage and tuning cost of LoRA, DreamBooth and textual inversion.

title: PuLID: Pure and Lightning ID Customization via Contrastive Alignment
claims: Tuning-free ID insertion that trains with a contrastive alignment loss plus an ID loss so the base model's behaviour is disturbed as little as possible.
Claims background, lighting, composition and style stay close to the output without the identity inserted.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext: Flow Matching for In-Context Image Generation and Editing in Latent Space
claims: The authors say earlier editing models lose character consistency and stability over several editing turns, and that Kontext keeps characters better in iterative edits.
Evidence is their own KontextBench (1,026 image-prompt pairs, five task types including character reference); no failure cases are listed in the abstract.

title: Concat-ID: Towards Universal Identity-Preserving Video Synthesis
claims: Encodes the reference image with the VAE and concatenates its features with the video latents along the sequence axis; reuses 3D self-attention, no extra modules.
Claims to beat prior methods for single and multiple identities and to extend to virtual try-on and background control.

title: DreamBooth: Fine Tuning Text-to-Image Diffusion Models for Subject-Driven Generation
claims: Fine-tunes a text-to-image model on a few images of a subject so a unique identifier binds to it, with a class prior-preservation loss.
The tuned subject can then appear in new scenes, poses, views and lighting not in the reference images.

title: Omni Reference (--oref)
claims: --oref takes a reference image of a character, object, vehicle or non-human creature; --ow weight runs 0 to 1000, default 100.
Use about 25 for style changes (photo to anime) and about 400 to keep a face or clothing; do not go above moderate values without very high --stylize or --exp.
At low weight, describe the features to keep in detail; two references for two characters is called somewhat untested.

title: Kling Element Library user guide
claims: A multi-image element is one main image plus 1 to 3 extras (2 to 4 total); the main image should be front-facing for higher consistency.
A video character element is a 3 to 8 second clip of one character, ideally with several angles; subject types include characters, animals, items, costumes, scenes.
Tips: give each element a unique name, describe core traits and what to ignore, add more angles for multi-view consistency, bind elements that appear in the start frame.

title: KLING VIDEO O1 user guide
claims: Up to 7 images or elements without a video input, 4 with a video; images JPG/PNG, at least 300 px, up to 10 MB; an element holds up to 4 images of one subject.
Refer to inputs in the prompt with @Image, @Video and @Element; describe each element, then interactions, environment, lighting.
For consistency: build elements from several angles, reuse the library across shots, reference every character explicitly in every prompt, keep lighting and style direction constant.

title: Ray3 Modify user guide
claims: Modify swaps the character in an input video (max 10 s) for a character reference image; the reference adapts to the video's style and lighting.
Strength runs from Adhere (keep shapes, good for retexture) to Reimagine (looser, for stylised or non-human characters); at the top the edges and background blur.
Reference mode works better at 1080p; the reference is called image1 or cref in prompts.

title: How to prompt Gemini 2.5 Flash Image generation for the best results
claims: If a character's features drift after many edits, start a new conversation and give a detailed description of the character.
For targeted edits, name only the element to change and say everything else stays the same.
With several input images of different aspect ratios the output takes the ratio of the last image.

title: Image generation with Gemini (Nano Banana)
claims: Up to 14 reference images per request: Gemini 3 Pro Image takes up to 5 character images, 6 object images and 3 style images; the 3.1 Flash models up to 4 characters and 10 objects.
The lightest model is stated as not optimised for multiple reference inputs or multi-turn editing.
notes: Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext image editing
claims: Kontext is said to hold character consistency over multiple edits; the example makes one change per prompt and refers to the subject by pronoun.
Scene changes such as place or weather are separate steps; output size follows the input (multiples of 32); a fixed seed gives repeatable results.
The page now recommends FLUX.2 for new projects, citing better editing and multi-reference support.

title: How do I create and use a Soul ID character
claims: Train on 20 to 80 photos of one person: varied angles and expressions, well lit, at least one full-height shot; no sunglasses, hats over the face, heavy shadow, crops or repeated poses.
A smaller clean varied set beats a large inconsistent set.
Result is the same person, not pixel-identical; extreme styles or odd angles drift slightly; one Soul ID is one person, so use Elements for several characters.

title: How many angles should a character reference sheet have
claims: Suggests six panels: front, side, profile, back, a face close-up and a mid-angle close-up, at 4K; the minimum for a simple character is a headshot plus a full-body view.
Remove props from the hands before the turnaround, generate several options and lock one before any video; make a new sheet for each look change.
Close-ups keep small details (scars, accessories) because video models invent what they cannot see.
notes: Vendor guide; one small team reportedly used 11 reference images for 4 characters and 1 prop.

title: Generate character turnarounds
claims: Prompt shape: style, then character description (features, outfit, expression), then a technical line such as 'character design sheet with multiple views (front, side, back), consistent lighting across all views'.
For complex characters make the front first, refine it, then use it as the reference for side and back views; keep pose influence 70 to 100 for aligned views.
Fix small inconsistencies in faces, hands or outfit with masking and inpainting.

title: How to use Veo 3.1 Ingredients to Video
claims: Up to three references (subject, environment, style); pick images of 1080p or more with a clean subject outline and an uncluttered background.
If the face drifts, the references may be too similar: use different angles (front and side profile); add explicit traits such as hair and eye colour to the prompt.
notes: Third-party guide, not Google.

title: AI video character consistency: keep the same face across every scene
claims: Use 3 to 5 references (front, three-quarter, profile) at 1024 px or more, same lighting and outfit across them, clean background.
Write a style guide (hair, eyes, build, skin, clothing, marks), repeat key features in every prompt, state what stays the same, and specify outfits because unspecified clothing gets improvised.
Change one variable per scene transition; save the best take early; repeated re-rolls accumulate variation, so stop after about 3 to 4.

title: The Build #1: How to create consistent AI characters
claims: Define age, face shape, hair, skin tone, wardrobe, posture precisely; vague definitions let the model improvise and drift starts.
Reuse the same phrasing, attribute order and vocabulary in every prompt; build a neutral turnaround (close-up, front, side, three-quarter, back) on a plain background.

title: Build consistent AI characters for video in 4 steps
claims: Make a hero image first, then one still per scene from it as a subject reference; animate each still in short 3 to 8 second clips and keep the best of four outputs.
Reusable description block: type, colours and texture, signature details, pose and framing, lighting and style.

title: Why AI video models fail when two characters interact
claims: When two characters share a frame the model blends face, hair and build into one hybrid.

Fix order: make characters visibly different (height, palette, body shape, costume silhouette), use multi-reference input (Kling up to four images), sketch the contact pose, film a rough mock, or cut together takes.
Reported budget: about three generations per usable shot and roughly 25% of takes used.
notes: Vendor FAQ with a creative director quoted.

title: Why start/end frame methods do not keep characters consistent
claims: Each generation is a fresh sample: start and end frames are loose guidance and faces, outfits and small props drift between clips.

Lock multi-angle sheets first (about five generations per lock); make a new sheet when outfit or injury changes; chain by giving the prior clip, character references and an environment plate together.
notes: Vendor FAQ.

title: Training a FLUX LoRA: dataset, captions and settings
claims: For a person or character use 15 to 30 sharp images; the model learns what stays constant, so vary backgrounds, lighting, distance and angle on purpose.
Short sentence captions with a rare trigger token; describe what varies (clothing, setting) and leave out the features to be learned.

About 50 to 100 steps per image; save checkpoints every few hundred steps; overfitting shows as repeated pose or background and failure to change clothing, fixed by an earlier checkpoint or LoRA weight 0.7 to 1.0.

title: How to fine-tune Wan 2.2 with an API
claims: Use at least 10 on-subject images or clips with a same-name .txt caption each; trim video clips to about 5 s; do not upscale source above 720p.
Default 400 steps and learning rate 0.0002; a rare trigger token in every caption; compare scale 0 and 1 on the same seed; try scale 0.6 to 0.9 if overbaked.
notes: Describes a generic subject or style trainer, not specifically characters.

title: The Chosen One: Consistent Characters in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
claims: Generates a batch from a text prompt, finds the group with a shared identity, extracts a tighter identity from it and repeats, with no reference images.
Claims a better balance of prompt fidelity and identity consistency than baselines, supported by a user study.
notes: Search summary (not the abstract) adds runtime of about 20 min per character and failure to keep supporting characters consistent.

title: MAGREF: Masked Guidance for Any-Reference Video Generation
claims: Several reference images go in through region-aware masks and channel concatenation; text-derived subject semantics are injected per region to cut confusion between subjects.
A four-stage data pipeline with varied training pairs targets copy-paste artifacts.

title: Video Storyboarding: Multi-Shot Character Consistency for Text-to-Video Generation
claims: Self-attention query features control identity as well as layout, so motion cannot be transferred without also transferring some identity.
A training-free Q-injection keeps identity across shots; later paper versions emphasise motion transfer more than multi-shot.

title: Lights, Camera, Consistency: A Multistage Pipeline for Character-Stable AI Video Stories
claims: Pipeline: an LLM writes a production script, a text-to-image model makes consistent character visuals, a video model uses them as anchors per scene.
Ablation: removing the visual anchors drops the consistency score from 7.99 to 0.55 (scale not given in the abstract).
notes: Under review; v1 only.

title: Identity-Preserving Image-to-Video Generation via Reward-Guided Optimization (IPRO)
claims: Image-to-video models lose the input person's identity with large expression change, big motion or a small face in frame.
Tunes the model with a face identity score as reward, with a KL regulariser; tested on Wan 2.2 I2V.

title: Slot-ID: identity from a reference video clip
claims: Single reference images give face deformation, identity drift and over-smoothed faces, because one image cannot show how identity changes over views and expressions.
Uses a short reference clip to distil identity tokens, with an image anchor; biggest gains under hard pose, expression and motion.
notes: Title shortened from the abstract page; the abstract does not use the phrase pose-locking.

title: EchoVideo: Identity-Preserving Human Video Generation by Multimodal Feature Fusion
claims: Names copy-paste artifacts and low similarity as the cost of leaning on low-level facial image information.
Fuses high-level text and identity-image features and randomly uses shallow face features in stage two, to ignore occlusion, pose and lighting of the reference.

title: GroundShot: anchors and visual memory for multi-shot consistency
claims: An entity's first clear appearance is its anchor and sets the consistency ceiling for later shots; drift is the slow divergence of reappearing entities.
Training-free agent: orders shots by usefulness as references, checks an entity before it enters memory, retrieves references before each shot; introduces GroundBench.
notes: Title shortened from the abstract page.

title: SkyReels-A2: Compose Anything in Video Diffusion Transformers
claims: Composes characters, objects and backgrounds from reference images with text; trains on prompt-reference-video triplets with an image-text joint embedding.
Introduces A2 Bench; claims the first open-source commercial-grade elements-to-video model.
notes: Another paper (AnyID) reports in search snippets that SkyReels-A2 copies reference clothing and background; not verified.

title: OpenS2V-Nexus: A Detailed Benchmark and Million-Scale Dataset for Subject-to-Video Generation
claims: OpenS2V-Eval has 180 prompts over seven subject-to-video categories and three automatic metrics: NexusScore (subject consistency), NaturalScore, GmeScore.
Evaluated 18 models; the dataset has 5 million 720p subject-text-video triplets.

title: Aura: Consistent Multi-Subject Video Generation via VLM-Grounded Semantic Alignment
claims: Adds subject-aware RoPE-Shift and learnable tokens to tell subject types apart and reduce copy-paste; a VLM is used as a conditioning encoder.
notes: Search snippets say a frozen VLM judge scores identity consistency and hard-copy per entity on 1 to 5; the abstract page does not show that.

title: Face Consistency Benchmark for GenAI Video
claims: Scores faces with six embedding models via DeepFace: cosine distance of each frame to a reference frame, or 200 random frame pairs; frames with no face are skipped.
ArcFace distance: real video 0.0843, Runway Gen-3 0.2346, HunyuanVideo 0.1734, CogVideoX1.5-5B 0.3005, Vchitect-2.0 0.4843 (lower is better), 30 videos per model.
No correlation with human judgement is reported.

title: Character references for consistent AI output
claims: A text description gives a different face each time; the reference fixes identity and the prompt controls the scene. For Sora 2 do not re-describe the character, it can clash with the reference.
Use a sharp frontal or three-quarter photo with hair and distinctive features visible, 2 to 3 extra views, test 3 to 5 images across scenes before production, reuse the same set.
For outfit consistency name the key garment in the prompt (for example 'wearing the same blue jacket').

title: AI video character consistency workflow
claims: A prompt gives the model a description, a reference gives it evidence; keep the video prompt short and about motion.
Checklist per clip: face shape and hairline, outfit and accessories, light temperature, style finish, whether the face holds through head turns.
Prefers defining a first frame and an end frame over simple last-frame chaining.

title: How to keep characters consistent in AI video
claims: Prompt pattern: a fixed identity line (age, face and hair, signature clothing) unchanged in every prompt, then a variable line for action, camera, setting, light.
Drift fixes: gradual face change means the wording shifted; different look per scene means no anchor reference; distortion in motion means shorten or calm the clip.
Compare every cut to the original reference, not just the previous clip; approve a clip before reusing a frame of it; fix drift before sound and grade.

title: Wan 2.2 prompting guide
claims: For image-to-video describe how things move (motion, camera, environment effects, speed), not what should appear; the image already sets the subject and scene.
Animate only what is visible; keep motion low on clothing; lock elements with anchors such as keeping the face still while hair moves.
notes: Third-party; not Alibaba's own guide.

title: Major identity drift and character consistency failure in video-to-video generation
claims: A user reports 20 to 30 tries in Google Flow where the face became a generic avatar even with a character profile, full-body and profile references attached.
Another user says even simple photo animation starts on the right face and the face changes significantly later; no official answer in the thread.
notes: Anecdotal; the product may have changed since.

title: Training-Free Consistent Text-to-Image Generation (ConsiStory)
claims: Shares internal activations across a batch through a subject-driven shared attention block and feature injection, with no optimisation step.
Claims state-of-the-art subject consistency and text alignment; extends to several subjects.

title: CANVAS: multi-agent storyboarding for long multi-shot narratives
claims: Enforces character continuity, persistent background anchors and location-aware planning; tested on ST-BENCH, ViStoryBench and new HardContinuityBench.
Reports gains over the best baseline of 21.6% background, 9.6% character and 7.6% props consistency.
notes: Title shortened from the abstract page.

title: PersonaShot: benchmarking person-centric narrative continuity in multi-shot video
claims: About 1,000 multi-shot segments, 16 metrics; character coherence tested within shots, across cuts and over sequences.
Finds a clear gap between perceptual quality and cross-shot continuity: visually strong videos reset characters' physical state between shots.
notes: Search summary adds that storyboard-guided systems held identity best; not in the abstract page.

title: OpenAI adds reusable characters and video stitching to Sora
claims: Sora characters extend cameos to pets, illustrations and toys as reusable avatars; the brief gives no creation steps or limits.
notes: Search summaries of other pages report a 3 to 10 second capture clip and two characters per video; not verified.

title: Runway Gen-4 References
claims: Search summary: references are used as image_1 to image_3, up to three; a clear face and costume in a simple setting gives steadier results than cluttered lifestyle references.

title: Seedream 4.0 (Freepik docs)
claims: Search summary: Seedream 4.0 takes up to 6 reference images (3.0 took 4) and keeps character identity and lighting better across batch outputs.
notes: No ByteDance primary page was reached.

title: Pika Scene Ingredients guide
claims: Search summary: Scene Ingredients combines your own images (reported up to six); advice is a clean well-lit reference, a prompt that spends more words on the character than the background, and 4 to 6 second clips.

title: How do I maintain character consistency in Dream Machine
claims: Search summary: 1080p can give better results with Character Reference; tag the main character with @character in a normal prompt.
notes: The page returned 404 when fetched.

title: Midjourney expands image control with Omni Reference
claims: Search summary: reports the --ow range and that Midjourney advises not going above medium values such as 400 without need because quality can degrade.
